# Sensitivity runs and ensembles: a single year

Many assessments have length data for one year only. FLicc then fits that
year (`years =`), and the uncertainty about the assumptions comes from
**sensitivity runs**: the same data refitted with one assumption changed at a
time. `fits_summary()` gives one table for a list of fits, and
`ensemble_flicc()` combines them into one estimate of SPR.

The reference fit and the sensitivity runs for the last year of the alfonsino
data: the gillnet with a dome (right-hand SD fixed at 0.85, 0.7 and 0.55 x
Linf), CVL 0.08 and 0.12, and Linf +/- 10%. `lapply()` runs one fit per value.

**Observation model for a single year: the multinomial.** The fits use
`obs_model = "mn"`. The Dirichlet-multinomial with estimated precision
(`dm_theta = "saturating"`, the default) estimates how much more variable the
compositions are than a multinomial sample of the same size, from the misfit
that remains after the fit. With one year that is one composition per gear: the
selectivity and F of each gear are fitted to that same composition, little
misfit is left over, and nothing shows overdispersion. The precision then runs
to its upper bound (FLicc reports this), the likelihood is flat in it, and the
convergence check fails (Hessian not positive definite). Over many years the
variation between years informs the precision; for one year it is not
estimable. For a single year, use

- `obs_model = "mn"` with a moderate effective sample size (`lfdess()`, about
  150-200 per gear, or in proportion to the number of samples, e.g. landings);
  raw counts of thousands of fish give intervals that are too narrow; or
- `obs_model = "dm"` with `dm_theta = "fixed"` (no precision to estimate;
  effective sample size about half the input); or
- with several gears in the same year, the estimated precision may work with
  `dm_shared = TRUE` (one precision for all gears), as there are then several
  compositions per precision parameter.

```{r one-year-fits}
yr <- 2024
set_ref <- list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "mn", FM_max = 4)

fit1 <- fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
               settings = set_ref, years = yr)

rsd <- c(dome_0.85 = 47, dome_0.7 = 39, dome_0.55 = 31)       # x Linf = 55.7
dome_runs <- lapply(rsd, function(r)
  fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = c("dsnormal", "dsnormal"), catch_by_gear = cbg,
         settings = set_ref, years = yr, sel_fixed = list(Gillnet = list(rsd = r))))

cvl <- c(CVL_0.08 = 0.08, CVL_0.12 = 0.12)
cvl_runs <- lapply(cvl, function(cv)
  fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
         settings = modifyList(set_ref, list(CVL = cv)), years = yr))

linf <- c(Linf_50 = 50.1, Linf_61 = 61.3)
linf_runs <- lapply(linf, function(li) {
  lh <- lhpar; lh["linf"] <- li
  fiticc(lfd, stocklen(lfd, lh, m_model = "constant"), sel_fun = sel_fun,
         catch_by_gear = cbg, settings = set_ref, years = yr)
})

runs1 <- c(list(reference = fit1), dome_runs, cvl_runs, linf_runs)
tab1 <- fits_summary(runs1)
tab1
```

**Residuals of a single year.** With one year, the residuals by length are the
residual plot (a bubble plot collapses to one column). Pearson and OSA
residuals of the reference fit:

```{r resid-singleyr, fig.height = 3.5}
plot_resid_len(fit1, type = "pearson")
plot_resid_len(fit1, type = "osa")
```

A run of residuals of one sign over several bins, in both types, means the
model cannot follow the composition at those lengths. With a single year it is
not possible to tell a year class from a selectivity misfit: both leave the
same pattern in one composition. The multi-year fit can separate them (section
*Residual diagnostics*). Residuals of a fit to one year also tend to be smaller
than 1 in sd, because the parameters are estimated from the same few data.



`fits_summary()` gives, for each run, the convergence (`conv`), SPR with its
confidence interval, F/M, apical F, Fspr40, current F relative to Fspr40, and
AIC with dAIC relative to the first run. Use only runs with `conv = "ok"`: a
run that fails is not a result (a typical failure: F slides to the lower bound
of F/M and SPR to almost 1, i.e. the composition is explained without fishing).
`r if (any(tab1$conv != "ok")) paste0("Here ", paste(tab1$run[tab1$conv != "ok"], collapse = ", "), " did not converge and is left out of the ensembles.") else "Here all runs converged."` AIC is
comparable between the runs because all use the same data and likelihood; a
change of data (e.g. a tail cut, another ESS) breaks this.

Two ensembles of the converged runs: equal weights, and Akaike weights:

```{r one-year-ensemble, fig.height = 4}
ok1 <- runs1[tab1$conv == "ok"]

ens_eq  <- ensemble_flicc(ok1, weights = "equal")
ens_aic <- ensemble_flicc(ok1, weights = "aic")
ens_eq$members
ens_aic$members
rbind(equal = ens_eq$table, aic = ens_aic$table)[, c("year", "spr", "lwr", "upr", "sd_within", "sd_between")]
plot_ensemble_flicc(ens_eq)
plot_ensemble_flicc(ens_aic)
```

With one year, `plot_ensemble_flicc()` shows each member and the ensemble as a
point with its interval. The two weightings answer different questions:

- **Equal weights** treat the runs as assumptions the data cannot decide
  between (a dome, Linf, CVL): the ensemble interval adds the spread between
  the runs (`sd_between`) to the uncertainty within each fit (`sd_within`).
  This is the usual choice for structural uncertainty.
- **Akaike weights** let the data decide. Here the AIC differences are small
  (at most `r round(max(ens_aic$members$dAIC), 1)`), so the weights spread over
  the runs and favour the domes. With large samples (many fish, or an ESS of
  500 per gear) AIC differences of 10 or more are common, and the best run then
  takes almost all the weight: the ensemble becomes a model selection. Use it
  as a check, and only for runs with the same data and likelihood. Linf in
  particular is informed mainly by the few largest fish, so AIC weights over
  Linf follow the tail of the composition rather than growth studies.

The same functions work for several years and for the dome levels of
`dome_sens_flicc()` (section *Dome sensitivity*).

**One fleet with two size modes.** When catch shares by gear are uncertain,
or for a quick single-fleet assessment, the gears can be pooled with
`combine_lfd()` (section *Exploring selectivity shapes*) and fitted as one
fleet. Its selectivity then has to describe both modes. The runs: logistic,
`"binormal"`, `"bidsnormal"`, and `"bidsnormal"` with a flat second mode
(`rsd2 = 1000` fixed). The pooled composition is rescaled to an ESS of 500 and
shows no overdispersion beyond it, so the Dirichlet-multinomial precision is
fixed (`dm_theta = "fixed"`); estimated, it runs to its upper bound and the
fits fail the convergence check:

```{r one-fleet-fits}

fit2gear <-fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
              settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating"))

lfd_fleet <- combine_lfd(lfd, catch_by_gear = c(0.95,0.05) ,
                         lhpar = lhpar, ess.n = 500)


stk_fleet <- stocklen(lfd_fleet, lhpar, m_model = "constant")




fleet_fun <- c(logistic = "logistic", binormal = "binormal",
               bidsnormal = "bidsnormal", bidsnormal_flat = "bidsnormal")
fleet_fix <- list(NULL, NULL, NULL, list(fleet = list(rsd2 = 1000)))

set_fleet <- modifyList(set_ref, list(dm_theta = "fixed"))

fleet_runs <- Map(function(fun, fix) {
  fiticc(lfd_fleet, stk_fleet, sel_fun = fun, catch_by_gear = 1,
         settings = set_fleet, sel_fixed = fix)
}, fleet_fun, fleet_fix)

tab_fleet <- fits_summary(c(list(ref2gear=fit2gear),fleet_runs))
tab_fleet
plot_compare_sel(fleet_runs)
```

```{r one-fleet-len, fig.height = 3.5}
ok_fleet   <- tab_fleet$conv == "ok"
best_fleet <- if (any(ok_fleet)) tab_fleet$run[ok_fleet][which.min(tab_fleet$AIC[ok_fleet])] else
  tab_fleet$run[which.min(tab_fleet$AIC)]
best_fleet
plot_len(fleet_runs[[best_fleet]])
```

```{r one-fleet-pars}
selpars_flicc(fleet_runs$bidsnormal)
selpars_flicc(fleet_runs$bidsnormal_flat)
```

AIC compares the fleet runs with each other (same pooled data), not with the
two-gear runs. A logistic curve cannot follow two modes: it reads the decline
after the first mode as fishing mortality. The free `"bidsnormal"` shows the
risk of six parameters on one year of data: its right limb runs to a very large
SD (`rsd2` of
`r round(as.numeric(selpars_flicc(fleet_runs$bidsnormal)[[1]]["rsd2"]))` cm), a flat
direction of the likelihood, and the fit fails. With `rsd2 = 1000` fixed
(`bidsnormal_flat`) the same shape converges: a first mode at about
`r round(as.numeric(selpars_flicc(fleet_runs$bidsnormal_flat)[[1]]["mode1"]))` cm and,
from about `r round(as.numeric(selpars_flicc(fleet_runs$bidsnormal_flat)[[1]]["mode2"]))` cm,
a plateau at the relative height `h`: the larger fish are retained at a
constant, lower level. A near-zero `lsd2` (a step up to the plateau instead of a
second mode) is typical when the data show no separate second mode; check
`selpars_flicc()` and `plot_compare_sel()` before using a two-mode fit.
`"binormal"` converges, but its SPR interval is wide.

SPR of the pooled runs spans
`r round(min(tab_fleet$SPR), 3)` to `r round(max(tab_fleet$SPR), 3)`, against
`r round(tab1$SPR[1], 3)` for the two-gear reference: with one fleet, the
selectivity curve and F share the information in one composition, and the
shape chosen for the large-fish mode decides how much of the decline is
attributed to fishing. The two-gear fit is preferable where the catch shares
are known: it keeps the selectivity of each gear, while pooling assumes that
each gear's sample represents its catch.
